Most formats do start with identifying 'magic' bytes (PNG signature, JPEG SOI marker FF D8, PDF '%PDF'), but many keep the table of contents at the END, not in a leading header: Parquet writes file metadata after the data, ZIP puts its central directory and end-of-central-directory record last, PDF locates its catalog via the trailer, and MP4 muxers usually write the moov index at the end unless 'faststart' moves it. MP3 has no global header; each frame carries its own header (ID3 metadata is a separate add-on).
precise_version: Most file formats begin with identifying bytes and keep metadata that tells the reader where each part of the file lies; that metadata sits in a header at the start or, in many formats (ZIP, Parquet, PDF, MP4 by default), in a footer at the end.

Correct. Minor: O-U-R-D-I-C-T is 7 letters; the board's OUR_DICT is exactly 8 bytes. Identifying leading bytes like this are what real formats call a signature or magic number (PNG's is 8 bytes).
The PNG signature is 8 bytes: hex 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A. Only bytes 2-4 spell 'PNG' (P-N-G, not P-N-N-G); the first byte is 0x89. The point that leading bytes identify the format is correct.
precise_version: Every PNG file starts with the same 8-byte signature (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A, which contains the letters 'PNG'), telling the decoder it is a PNG.

JPEG/JFIF files are a stream of marker-identified segments (SOI FF D8, an APP0 'JFIF' segment, then image data); a still JPEG is one image, not a sequence of frames like video. In MP4 the index of where audio and video samples lie (the moov box) is usually written at the END by muxers unless moved to the front with 'faststart'. Audio tracks hold compressed coded audio, not a raw waveform.
Correct as stated for this context.

Parquet starts with a 4-byte magic number 'PAR1', but its real metadata (schema, row groups, column-chunk locations) is a footer: file metadata, then its 4-byte length, then 'PAR1' again at the end. The docs say metadata is written after the data 'to allow for single pass writing', and readers read the metadata first to find the column chunks they need.
precise_version: Parquet also stores metadata that tells readers where each column chunk lies, but it keeps it in a footer at the end of the file (after a leading 'PAR1' magic number), not in a header.

note: Right that JSON has no header or index: a JSON text is just a sequence of tokens (JSON-text = ws value ws), so finding a key means parsing sequentially. Streaming parsers can stop early and need not build the whole in-memory dictionary, but there is still no way to jump straight to an entry.

RFC 4180 allows an optional CSV header line (column names), signalled by the MIME parameter header=present/absent; that is a header in a different sense (column names, not metadata saying where sections lie). PDF does start with a '%PDF' version header, but its catalog is located through the trailer at the end of the file.
